title.en: Lumawig on Earth: The Bean Miracle, the Wedding Feast, and the Man in the Rock
title.zh: 盧馬維格在人間：豆莢奇蹟、婚宴與石化於岩中者

region.en: Bontoc, Mountain Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Igorot tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋山省博托克（伊哥洛特故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Igorot: 'Lumawig on Earth', eBook #12814

summary.en: Lumawig the Great Spirit comes down to marry the girl Fukan, filling her bean baskets from a single pod, enlarging her chickens and pigs, and outdoing her mocking brother-in-law at the wedding feast. When the brother-in-law quarrels over water, Lumawig strikes a rock to create it and thrusts him into the rock, where his body becomes a spring; before returning to the sky Lumawig sets his wife afloat in a coffin that reaches Tinglayen, where a widower finds and marries her.
summary.zh: 大神盧馬維格下凡娶富坎，一豆莢滿其籃，令雞豬速大，於婚宴上戲弄譏諷之舅兄。舅兄因水起爭執，盧馬維格以矛擊石出水，將其推入岩中，其身軀化為泉源。臨歸天前，盧馬維格置妻於棺浮水，棺漂至丁格拉延，為鰥夫所拾並娶之。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Igorot narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Igorot communities. The tale ends by etiologically explaining springs in rocks and a local place (Tinglayen), so a sacred-place motif tag is used.

passages.text: One day Lumawig, the Great Spirit who dwells in the sky, looked down and saw two sisters gathering beans, and he came down to visit them. When the younger sister Fukan told him how slow their work was, he asked for a single pod of beans, shelled it into the basket, and the basket was at once full. He filled another basket the same way, and when Fukan fetched three more, he filled them all. Her father, hearing the story of the young man who could fill a basket from one pod, said, "Go bring the young man here, for I think he must be a god." Lumawig helped carry the beans home, and when the father gave him water in a cocoanut shell he said, "If I stay here with you, I shall become very strong."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumawig on Earth'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next morning Lumawig fed the family's one hen and chicks rice meal, and as they ate they grew until they were cocks and hens; he fed the pigs sweet potato leaves, and they too grew to full size. The delighted father offered his elder daughter in marriage, but Lumawig chose the younger, Fukan. When the brother-in-law sneered that there was no rice, beef, pork, or chicken for a wedding feast, Lumawig answered, "I shall provide our wedding feast." He hurled two great pine trees to Lanao for the fire, set ten kettles boiling, and filled five of them full by passing one small basket of rice over them. He called deer and pigs from the forest for the people to catch, and though the brother-in-law chased the finest pig until he was exhausted, he could not seize it until Lumawig lifted it for him; then the pig cut loose and escaped twice more, until Lumawig himself carried it back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumawig on Earth'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After the feast they consulted the omen for the northern tribes, and when the hot, thirsty people asked Lumawig to create water, the brother-in-law taunted him for caring nothing for their thirst. They quarreled, and Lumawig told the people to rest; while they rested he struck the rock with his spear and water flowed out. The brother-in-law leaped to drink first, but Lumawig held him back and made him drink last; then he gave him a push that sent him into the rock, and water came from his body. "You must stay there," said Lumawig, "because you have troubled me a great deal," and they left him in the rock. Some time later Lumawig returned to the sky, first placing his wife in a wooden coffin with a dog at her feet and a cock at her head, bidding the coffin float without stopping until it reached Tinglayen. A widower sharpening his ax on the bank fished it out; Fukan cried out not to drive a wedge, and as the widower had no wife, he married her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Lumawig on Earth'; not verbatim.

title.en: How the First Head Was Taken
title.zh: 第一顆人頭如何被取下

region.en: Bontoc, Mountain Province, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Igorot tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋山省博托克（伊哥洛特故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Igorot: 'How the First Head was Taken', eBook #12814

summary.en: Kabigat the Moon, a woman, is molding a copper pot when a son of Chal-chal the Sun stops to watch her work. Annoyed by his staring, she strikes him with her paddle and cuts off his head, but the Sun hurries from afar, sets the head back on, and the boy lives again; the Sun then decrees that because of this act, people will forever cut off one another's heads on the earth.
summary.zh: 月神卡比加特為女性，正以拍打之法塑造銅釜；太陽查爾查爾之子駐足觀看。月神厭其凝視，以槳擊之，斬落其首；太陽遙知此事，趕至現場，將頭顱安回，男孩復生。太陽遂下斷言：因此事之故，世人從此將互相取下人頭。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Igorot narrators; presented as an archival record. The story etiologically explains headhunting as a consequence laid on humankind by the Sun's decree; the Thompson-style taboo-transgression tag is an interpretive mapping (an act of violence whose consequence endures as a law of the world), noted here because the European motif index has no exact equivalent.

passages.text: One day the Moon, who was a woman named Kabigat, sat in the yard making a large copper pot. The copper was still soft and pliable like clay, and she squatted on the ground with the heavy pot against her knees while she patted and shaped it, pressing a stone against the inside and pounding the outside with a wooden paddle dripping with water until she had worked down the bulges and formed a smooth surface. A son of Chal-chal the Sun came by and stopped to watch her mold the form, standing still for some time, for he was greatly interested in seeing the jar grow larger, more beautiful, and smoother with each stroke. Suddenly the Moon looked up and saw him watching her, and instantly she struck him with her paddle and cut off his head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How the First Head was Taken'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sun was far away, but he knew as soon as the Moon had cut off his son's head. Hurrying to the spot, he put the boy's head back on, and he was alive again. Then the Sun said to the Moon, "You cut off my son's head, and because you did this ever after on the earth people will cut off each other's heads." In this way the tale explains the beginning of head-taking among the Igorot: the first severed head was that of the Sun's own son, taken not in war but in a moment of anger at a potter's wheel, and the custom follows from that first blow as its consequence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'How the First Head was Taken'; not verbatim.

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Igorot: 'The Serpent Eagle', eBook #12814

summary.en: Two boys sent daily for firewood are starved and scolded by their mother no matter what wood they bring. Driven to despair, the elder climbs a tree and calls down "Here is some wood" as his own arm bones, leg bones, and finally all his bones drop to the ground; the younger carries the bundle of bones home, and the elder, transformed into a serpent eagle, flies overhead and cries that he no longer needs her food.
summary.zh: 兩兄弟每日為母拾柴，無論所拾為何皆受責罵且不得飽食。長兄絕望之餘攀上大樹，喊「這是柴火」，其臂骨、腿骨乃至全身骨骼紛紛落地。弟弟背起骨柴回家，長兄化為蛇鷹，盤旋於母親頭頂，啼叫自己不再需要她的食物。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Igorot narrators; presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Igorot communities. Transformation tag marks the elder brother's becoming of a serpent eagle; the tale also etiologically explains the bird's cry.

passages.text: Two boys were sent by their mother every day to the forest to get wood for her fires. Each morning she gave them a little poor food for the trip, saying the wood they brought the day before was too poor to earn more. If they brought nice pine wood she scolded them; if they brought large dry reeds she said these were no good because they left too much ashes in the house. Try as they would, they failed to satisfy her, and their bodies grew very thin from working all day and from want of enough to eat. One morning she gave them a bit of dog meat, and the boys were very sad as they set out for the mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Serpent Eagle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the forest one brother told the other to wait while he climbed a tree to cut branches. From above he called "Here is some wood," and the bones of his arm dropped to the ground. "Here is some more wood," and the bones of the other arm fell; then the bones of his legs, and so on, until all the bones of his body lay on the ground. "Take these home," he said, "and tell the woman that here is her wood; she only wanted my bones." The younger boy, alone and weeping, gathered up the bundle. As he finished, a serpent eagle called down from the treetops, "I will go with you, Brother," and the bird flew over the boy's head all the way home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Serpent Eagle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the mother looked at the wood she was very much frightened and ran out of the house. The serpent eagle circled round and round above her head, crying "Quiukok! quiukok! quiukok! I do not need your food any more." The tale thus explains both the origin of the serpent eagle and the meaning of its call, told as a warning against mothers who starve the children who serve them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Serpent Eagle'; not verbatim.

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Igorot: 'The Tattooed Men', eBook #12814

summary.en: Two young friends, unhappy that neither has been tattooed, agree to mark each other. One works carefully over his friend's breast, back, arms, legs, and face, rubbing in soot so that he is beautifully tattooed; the other, taking revenge or jest too far, scrapes a great pile of pot soot and rubs it over his friend head to foot. They fight, and the beautifully tattooed one becomes a great lizard that hides in the tall grass while the sooty one becomes a crow that flies away over the village.
summary.zh: 兩位年輕摯友因未曾紋身而鬱鬱，相約互為對方紋身。一人細心為友在胸背、四肢、臉上刺紋並擦入鍋底煙灰，友人因而俊美；另一人卻刮起一大堆煙灰，將其從頭到腳塗滿全身。二人相鬥，俊美者忽化巨蜥遁入深草，滿身煙黑者化為烏鴉飛越村莊而去。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Igorot narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological tale of lizard and crow plumage and of tattooing customs.

passages.text: Two young men, very good friends, were unhappy because neither of them had been tattooed, and they felt they were not as beautiful as their friends. One day they agreed to tattoo each other. One marked the breast and back of the other, his arms and legs, and even his face; then he took soot from the bottom of a cooking-pot and rubbed it into all the marks, and the man was tattooed beautifully. The one who had done the work said, "Now, my friend, you are very beautiful, and you must tattoo me."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Tattooed Men'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the newly tattooed man scraped a great pile of black soot off the cooking-pots, and before the other knew what was happening, he had rubbed it all over him from the top of his head to the bottom of his feet, leaving him black and greasy. Covered with soot, the man grew very angry and cried, "Why do you treat me so when I tattooed you so carefully?" They began to fight, but suddenly the beautifully tattooed one became a great lizard which ran away and hid in the tall grass, while the sooty one became a crow and flew away over the village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Tattooed Men'; not verbatim.

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Igorot: 'Tilin, the Rice Bird', eBook #12814

summary.en: A little girl begs raw rice while her mother pounds the evening meal, and is scolded for talking too much. Left alone while the mother fetches water, she lifts the winnower covering the basket of rice; the cover slips, she falls, and she is covered up inside. When the mother hears a bird crying from the basket and removes the cover, a little brown rice bird hops out, flying away and calling goodbye to the mother who would not give it any rice to eat.
summary.zh: 小女孩在母親舂晚餐米糧時討要生米，反被斥責多話。母親取水離家後，她掀開米籃上的簸箕蓋；蓋子一滑，她跌入籃中為米所覆。母親回來聽見籃中傳出鳥啼，掀蓋一看，一隻小棕雀跳出，一面飛去一面回頭喊道：再見，媽媽；你不肯給我米吃。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Igorot narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological tale of the rice bird (tilin) and its cry.

passages.text: One day a mother was pounding out rice to cook for supper when her little girl ran up crying, "Oh, Mother, give me some of the raw rice to eat." The mother said no, that it was not good for her until it was cooked, and told her to wait for supper. But the girl persisted until the mother, out of patience, cried, "Be still. It is not good for you to talk so much!" When the rice was pounded, the woman winnowed it, emptied it into her basket, covered it with the winnower, and set off to the spring for water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Tilin, the Rice Bird'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The little girl loved to go to the spring with her mother and play in the cool water, but this time she stayed behind, and as soon as the woman was out of sight she ran to the basket of rice and reached down to take a handful of grain. The cover slipped so that she fell, and was covered up in the basket. When the mother returned, she heard a bird crying "King, king, nik! nik! nik!" and, listening carefully, found the sound came from the basket. She removed the cover, and to her surprise a little brown rice bird hopped out. As it flew away it kept calling back, "Goodbye, Mother; goodbye, Mother. You would not give me any rice to eat."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Tilin, the Rice Bird'; not verbatim.
